blocks.x: I'll make a note on here that we're interviewing Mr. Earl Foster, this is Bill Russell, and Ralph Collins is here, and also Mr. Harold Dajon. And the date is March the 22nd, 1961. What is the address here? 3212 Borough. Do you mind giving your full name, Mr. Foster?
Earl Foster.
Any middle name?
Yes, no. Earl Foster.
Were you born right here in New Orleans?
Born in Manville, Louisiana.
Open Manville, I hope you're in.
Oh, I'll go off.
Do you mind telling us the date, your birthday?
December 28th, 1904.
1904. Yes. Did your parents play any music, your father or mother or anyone else in the family?
No. Well, it was just a northern minister.
He was a minister?
Yes.
Do you remember, what kind of a church was it?
It was a Baptist. Baptist. Yes, Baptist Church of Manville, Louisiana.
Do you remember any special music in the church when you were young? What kind of music and singing they had?
No, I sang in the church. You did sing? Yeah, in Baptist Church. Yes. In Manville, Louisiana. Then I stayed at the Arnold Turtle during the year of, I'll say, about 22. See?
You stayed over on that side of the lake?
Yeah. And I came in to a north here. Went to work. Then I got drums. See?
Were the drums your first instrument?
Drums were first instrument, yes. Oh, yeah. Drums were really first instrument.
Did you take any lessons on drums?
Not on drums. I take a lesson on sax.
Well, when you first took off the drums, you took them up here in New Orleans?
I take a bunch of drums here and went over to the same boy, Harold Peterson. The first man they showed me, they had the whole drum stick.
The one has the music store?
Yeah, pizza. And then I came on back to New Orleans, you know what I'm saying? Yeah. And then started to, I went with different fellows here in New Orleans.
In 1923 is when you started playing.
Yeah, when you started playing. With Amos Rowley. With Amos Rowley. That's the first band.
The first band was Amos Rowley.
Amos Rowley, yeah.
And who was the members of the band?
The members was this boy, Big Island, he played piano. I got more of that.
Go ahead and tell you Sam.
Sam Dutre. And they had a fellow by the name of Pope play trombone.
Is that Sam Dutre? Is that the young son or the old man?

No, it was his father, the old man. The old man. And Orange Kelly played trombone. And Orange Kelly played trombone. Yeah, Orange Kelly. And they had another fellow by the name of, Lee Dutton played bass. Emerson played trumpet. Then he had a fellow played, played saxophone by the name of Harris. Which is your Harris?
No, no. He sang horn playing with Willie James.
That's what, when I had my old man. Yeah. That's what my old man, Willie James. Are you speaking about Amos Rowley?
Old man Dutre. Dutre playing with him, yeah.
With Amos Rowley. Yeah.
Sam Dutre, the old man. Old man Dutre. Who was he playing?
Clarinet.
Clarinet. The old man off those saxophone.
Clarinet, yeah.
And who was the piano player?
Called, we, his name was Lewis. We called him Big Eye Lewis.
It wasn't, I knew the clarinet player, Big Eye Lewis. No, not that. It was downtown.
It was downtown. It was downtown.
It was downtown.
It was downtown on Cater Street.
And they called him Big Eye Lewis? Big Eye Lewis, yeah. I never knew that. I knew him.
He was a piano player. I don't know him. He was a piano player. He was a piano player. He died.
And what's your last name?
Lewis Robinson.
Lewis Robinson.
That's right. Lewis Robinson.
Did you mention a gentleman by the name of Pork or something? Did you say some name like that?
Yeah, well, Pork was a trombonist. Up to the top of the drum.
Oh, Ernest Kelly. Yeah. His nickname was Pork.
No, Pork is, that's a different, that's, I made a mistake in here. He played trombonist too. He was the author of the original band that we had, about seven pieces, see. And that's.
Amos Riley's band.

Amos Riley's band, yeah. And we played. And we played. Banjo. Yeah, no, Willie Bonkian on banjo. Willie Bonkian. Willie Bonkian on banjo. Oh, yes. Yeah. We played the Chester Club, the Boston Club, the Western Church Club, the Southern United Club, all places like that, you know.

Can you tell us anything more about the music over across the lake, before you came over? Oh. Did they have many dances over there? I guess you didn't go to many dances if you were raised there in the church at first.

Yeah, they had dances over there. They had the Southern Dollars Hall, I said that, but they had dances. And this same boy, I'll speak about, I will tell you a little later about that, what it be a tea, you know. Yeah. That's where he used to come and play. That's in Mandelville.
Did they have any bands in Mandelville? Any Mandelville bands?

Oh, yeah, they had the Independent Band, which was Isidore Fritz. George Lewis has told me about that. Yeah, that's right. Isidore Fritz and Clarence. Yeah, the Clarence. Some Clarence too, but they had the Independent Band. And you remember anybody else in the Independent Band? In the Band? Like the Trumon Flair from over there. Oh, let me see now. Fat fella, big fat fella.
Cheek used to go to that Blit Affair whatever you have before he died. Dan Mooney. Yeah, Dan Mooney.
Yeah, Dan Mooney. Yeah, Dan Mooney. They had a trumpet player by the name of Leonard Parker.
That's right. And he was a little bit of a trumpet player. They had a trumpet player by the name of Leonard Parker. That's right.

And he was a trumpet player by the name of the 된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된 He was a great kind of Dixon-aim man especially. That's right.
Did he read much, do you know, or was it all a head...
He read, but he had a lot of stuff. His own ideas. He had lots of... He had a lot of his own ideas.
What was his tone like? Was he sort of rough or was he fast?
He was a fast man. He was smooth and fast. That's right. He was what you would say an artist on a planet. That's right. He was an old place. You didn't know him.
Is anybody around here sounding like him? I've heard of him, but I don't remember listening at him playing.
He and me see.
Did he sound like, say, George Lewis or Louis Cottrell or...
You might as well say Contreras.
More like that.
More like Cottrell. Yeah, it was something like that. But he was all around. He was Dixieland. He played sweet, hot. He was on, you know...
On ideas.
On ideas. And play what you put in front of him. So he was a great clan. He didn't know him. He's dead now, but that's what he was.
You know when he died about?
He's dead now about... Oh, I would say at least about... Easy, I'd say. About six years.
Not so awfully long then.
Yeah.
I believe Andy Anderson said he came from that. The trumpet player, you know? That's my cousin, yes. Oh, so you knew him then? Yes.
He plays trumpet. He plays band. Oh, yes. That's right.
Another trumpet player that left here very early, Tommy Ladner. Yeah, he died in New York. Did you ever know him?
Yes, Tommy, yes. He played trumpet there. Great blues king. Yeah.
Did you remember him when you were a kid?
I remember him when you were a kid. That's right. Heard him play? Heard him play, oh yes. Tommy, yes.
Because he left here so long ago, most people down here don't even know who you're talking about when you mention him. He was the great blues king over there.
That's where he started at, right over there.
Yeah.
On that trumpet. Tommy Ladner, that's right. His mother was named Willie Madner.
I think Bunk Johnson told me once he used to go over there and play with Isidore Fritz. Bunk Johnson went over there and played with him. That was before 1914, about that time.

That was about 1915 or 16. You'd be about 10 or 11 years old. I just remember them, but I remember him, Bunk Johnson, coming over there. When Isidore Fritz. Well during that time Tommy played with them too.
Yeah, I know. That's what I heard. Tommy Ladner played with them too.
Tommy Ladner was younger than them. Yeah. Tommy Ladner played with the players. He was a great blues man. I met him in New York. I got to hear him. Yeah. Yeah.

He was a great blues man. That's right. I was like that. Yeah. Any other music over there that you can remember? Any other good bands like that? Even if they weren't that good, what other bands that they have can you remember? Who's there? They have a band right close there in Madisonville.
No, the Christian band lived there from Madisonville, you know. Yeah. That's the only band they had during those days.
Do you remember any music on the boats that went back and forth on the lake? What? Like the Camellia or any other boats that you can remember?

Yeah. The Camellia had bands from New Orleans, which was, I don't remember them, I didn't know them since I was playing, you know who they were. That's Joy John, you know, bass player and Walter Preston, which he was a guy.
I think Wooden Joe, he only worked on the Camellias one while. Wooden Joe.

Joe Nicholas. Wooden Joe, yeah, and Joy John and Walter Preston, band of us. That's from New Orleans, yeah. They were from New York to come over on the Camellia. We were kids, but I remember them coming over and playing.
Did you get to hear any of that music? Did you hear it from the showers? Oh yeah, you could hear the music.
Gary, I remember I was a little boy, I listened to their band lots of times, especially on Sundays. They were really Chilain fellas, Wooden Joe.
I know some of the musicians tell me they used to come over, or used to go over there to Mandeville for picnics and things. Do you remember much of that kind of thing going on when you were a boy?

Well, that was during, I think, the 7th at a time then. Even that then? Yeah, that was during, well that was, that was in the 20th then. That was in the 20th. Yeah, that was during the 20th when the band was for one of the big pieces. I know, bands from New Orleans, yeah.

Do you remember any parades, brass bands over there when you were a boy? Did they ever have a parade like they have them over here almost every Sunday in the summer, and funerals and everything? Did they ever have anything like that over there?

Oh yeah, they had them, but I can't remember. Back to that, I don't remember. Yeah, I know it was a long time ago. Yeah, the band was over there for them. And the independent band, which was the little Prince and Thomas, Thomas Leidenier. That's right. They played them.
They played parades or funerals too?
No, not funerals, but they played parades. Oh, parades.
Oh, that's right.

Prince. During those days, I can recall, the band didn't parade like they parade now, you know, the band's riding what you call it, Cattleho, you know? The band's riding and riding and playing the parades, you know? Oh yeah, they played parades, I was a boy, but I don't remember. They seen Bunk Johnson. Bunk Johnson played parades over there. Bunk, you know? Yeah, sure.
They ride, what do you mean, they ride in a truck?

They ride in a Cattleho, they call it in those days. What is that? Oh, it's like a big bus. But it's open, you know, open, with what I'd say rods on the side of it. And the band's riding the truck and the people walk, see? The band, they walk like the band's here, the Cattleho's Parades, the Cattleho's Parades.
Is that a horse farm man?
No.
A regular motor, yeah.

A regular motor. That's right. A regular motor. That's the fifth, the Indian Pound band. And Bunk Johnson was a strongman. He used to call me, he's the one giving me a nickname, or Brother, see? You know, they used to call me Brother. Bunk Johnson. Bunk Johnson, yeah. You know Bunk Johnson, you know him? Well I didn't know him, though.
I knew him quite well in New York and down here, too.
Down here, too, yeah. Made records of him many years ago, fifteen years ago.
Yeah. That's where he was here. That's where he had left him over there. Yes, yes. Well he came over, he came from, how do I think, Charlie, Charlie.
New Iberia, you went out that way, Texas and every place. He lived all through there.
Yeah, he lived all through there, yeah.
So you came over across the lake then about when you were 1922 or so you said?
Yeah, in 1922. I came here too long.
And you hadn't played music though yourself before then? I got my drums. Well you already had your drums. I got my drums over there.

Got my drums in 1922. Got my drums in 1921. In 1921 I got drums, yeah. And I came over here. And I played with the first band in the Amos Raleigh over here, before I formed a home group. And Sam was Raleigh. And the men that I called him, you know. Yes, all those other men.
Yeah. Who were some of the best bands here when you got here, that you first heard when you came over?
The lead band was Celestine.
Celestine. Celestine. Kid Rainey. Sam Morgan, right?

That's right. Sam Morgan, Kid Rainey, the band that I met. Celestine. The first band I had was Celestine. Kid Rainey, Sam Morgan, Andrews at the same time. But it was these two. I wasn't strong enough to play with them at all. You know. Yes. That's right. That's right. Well when you formed your band, who did you have in your band?
Well, I formed my band.

I had the same couple of players, Andrew Anderson. You understand? Andrew Anderson. James Miller on piano. And Willie James on classical saxophone. And this boy, Austin Youngs, that's the bass player.
Oh yes, I knew him.
But, you knew him? He left Sidney Desby's band to come with me. That's great. Mm-hm.
And he stilled me until he died. And he played bass then? He played bass and trombone. Yeah. Bass and trombone.
I knew he played trombone. I never heard him on trombone. He lost his tape at the time I knew him.

Yeah, he was a great bass player. And ran for the band. He kept the group going until he died. That's right. He started to tell my mother about it. I said, if he's dead, four years. I don't think he's dead four years.
He was dead when I moved here five years ago. He died just shortly before.
He died. He'd been going around six or seven years.
More like six, I think.
Yeah, between six and seven.
I didn't even know he wasn't living when I moved here in 1956. He was living then, wasn't he?
That's Boots you're talking about.
Yeah, the bass player.
Boots, yeah. Boots been dead six or seven years.
The other was Sport, the sax player.
Oh, Sport's brother. Yeah. It's Sport's brother voice, yeah. On the Pointerville.
It's Sport's brother voice. Yeah. It's Sport's brother voice.
What's Boots right now?
Austin Young.
Austin. Austin Young, yeah. He played good drum.
Good drum. Yeah, in the Fusyville City a long time.
When was that you formed your band?
We played together a long time. This part right here. When did you play with her on the country? I played drums. What band was that?
Who's? Oh, that's a long time ago. I was small. He grew 20th ways to come in. Yeah, I see. Well, when was that you formed your band first? No, 1923 you were then? No, I left.

Buddy died. I'm not. Let me see. No, not 23. No, indeed. Buddy died, 32. That's when Buddy died in 32 July the 4th. Buddy B. T. I played Buddy B. T.'s band after Amos Rowley, you see. Oh, I see. I played Amos Rowley's band regularly. And then Amos died.
How long were you with Amos Rowley?

I was with Amos, I'd say at least seven years. Oh, I see. After Amos Rowley died, then he joined Buddy B. T.'s band. I joined Buddy B. T.'s band. On drum. He joined Buddy B. T.'s band. Who else was in Buddy B. T.'s band? I think of Chester Lazzard as a bass band. And Manny Gabriel on Clownette. He had a film on by Eddie Morris. He still lives. Oh, yes. He still lives. Yeah, he still lives. It's hard to think of those fellas right. He was a guitar player?
Huh? He was in a guitar or a band or a band or a band? Yes.

Yes, he was this old time with Freddie Keppert. Freddie Keppert. Oh, no, Louis Keppert. Louis Keppert. That's Freddie Keppert. I don't know. I don't remember Freddie Keppert. Yeah. But Louis Keppert. Yes. That's when I went to the band. Who was playing guitar? Or banjo. You was playing banjo. Yeah. Louis Keppert. That's right. That's the guitar player.
Then you say, I think before Manny was playing clarinet, whatever, who that was playing clarinet was playing? Mani Gabriel. Before Mani Gabriel. There was another clarinet player.
Let me see. Let me see.
Let me see. Yeah, you said that Isidro Prince played with him a while too. Before Mani Gabriel. That's right.

Isidro Prince played with him too, yes. But before Mani, Isidro Prince. Did Isidro Prince come over on the side? Yes, indeed. That's the buffum over the lake I'm talking about. He came over there? Yeah. Yeah. He played for me to go over there and play.
Oh, I remember somebody told me once that Buddy used to play a lot across the lake too. Sometime.
He played right over there and played. A lot of white encarners over there.
Like he might have had a home over there even. Do you remember that? Did he ever live over there? He did live over there. He did?
He did a while. That's right. That's right.
That's right.

Oh yeah, listen boy, we forget after this fellow, Louis Kepard. We must never forget Buddy Mallory. Yeah. And the Arnold was on too. He went and lived over there. He's from right here, right downtown, right in the district, you know. Buddy. He played with him a long time. That's who came with him. During the time when I came with him, Buddy Mallory came with him. Oh yeah. Because he and this boy, I don't know if something happened. The lawyer was supposed to go play with Celestine, see. Anyway, he got this boy Buddy Mallory. He died until he died. There's an old picture that Edmund Hall, the clarinetist, he's in New York now.

We played with Armstrong different people a few years ago. But Edmund Hall had this picture, I think, of the band across the lake with Buddy Petit and Mandeville. And I forget my word about that. Mandalay, I mean. No, Buddy Mallory, that's a guitar player. Yeah.
A banjo player.
George Washington was on. George on Tramon.
George on Tramon, that's right. And Chester was on bass. Chester on bass, that's right.
Let's see, I can't remember, there was a singer there, but nobody knew his name in the picture. Do you remember any special singer over there that might have been singing?
I always wanted to sing with him, me. I always wanted to sing with him. You were right. I hadn't taught the page of him yet, that's right. I wanted to sing with him.

Look at that picture again. Yeah. Yeah, I was talking about him. I wasn't a fan of the other night, that's right. Do you know that picture of me? I was in a Eureka. No, I was just in a Eureka. It was published in Esquire once, two years ago. It was in a Eureka.

That was me. That made me sing. Yeah. That's right. Megaphone, megaphone. Yeah, that's you. That's you. That's you, brother. Do you remember that photograph being taken? You sure have a megaphone? Yeah, yeah, yeah. Sure you have that. Yeah. What it was crazy for me, he was, you know, the opportunity.
Do you remember anybody taking your photograph at any time?
They take that picture a lot of times over there.
On the other side?
Over the other side, yeah. I can't remember.
Were you playing drums at that time? I was singing.

You were singing? I hadn't started playing drums. You hadn't started playing drums. I hadn't started playing drums. Who was playing drums? I wasn't playing drums. I was singing. The boy is gay, boy. Yeah. Well, I don't call him. I don't remember now. I forget. Rick Carl's brother.
Rick Carl's brother? Rick Carl's brother.
Rick Carl's brother. Rick Carl's brother. Rick Carl's brother. Rick Carl's brother.
Yeah? That's right.
How'd he call him? I can't call his name. I don't know. He married one of my cousins. He did.
I can't tell you. From Bay St. Louis or over in that right? He's from Bay St. Louis.
That's right. He's from Bay St. Louis. That's right. He was living there with Rick Carl.
He was, yeah. In fact, they all came away from the fleet. You understand? I thought I'd get that now.
You see?
Put it on there. Yeah. You got the phone right there. Yeah. He says the boy's name. Now, let me see.
Got it on the tip of my tongue. It was short of my own. He was playing with Buddy at that time.
He was the drummer. That's right. But I couldn't call his name right now. I know his brother Rick Carl. Rick Carl. His brother's name. Do you remember him? A bass player. Yeah.
We interviewed him and he told us about his family. So I guess his name, we'll have his name in the interview.
You mean he was supposed to play the trumpet? Yeah.
He played trumpet and then played bass then.
Yeah. Played bass then. Now, this is when he was dead. I don't know if you remember him. He died. That's what I'm talking about. Played drums. The other brother. No.
I never knew.
He did now, I imagine, about ten years.
Was that Buddy's regular band at that time with Edmund Hall and Chester?
Well, let me get it straight now about the children who were playing trombone.
He said he loved that.
I don't think Edmund was in the band at the time. About seventh grade stuff Everyone came over there at the time, wasn't it? I don't think he was a member of the band, was he?

Well, he's in the photograph with Buddy, but I wondered if he was just playing perhaps that one day, or if he was a regular member, or if Buddy had a regular band, or did he just pick up for that regular band?

He was playing with Buddy, and he was playing with Buddy, and he was playing with Buddy. And I told Buddy I was playing, I had my drums, and he was surprised. I made him on a big Sunday night. I mean, a big Monday night we played at Cheshire Club, and it was Rowley. I was playing with him. He was the same old man that didn't go to the John Rubin Show. They were surprised to see, because John Rubin Show knew when I came here. He was the same old man that didn't go to the John Rubin Show. You remember him? Go ahead.
I never knew, I heard of him a lot.
That's when I had told him I had got my drums, you know. And I started out playing. Well, I played with embers. And they were embers, the embers, and he died. Right there on the yellows' feet.
What kind of a drum set did you have when you started out? How big a set was it, and what kind of drums?
I had one of those big old yellow 26 inch bass drums.
Remember what make it was?

Wallachs. Wallachs. Rudolph Wallachs. I set the cistern out and got it. Well, it's a realtor. It was. Yeah, and that drum was exactly six months getting here. See, that drum was six months getting... Yeah? Yeah. Well, getting to Mandeville. Wow. That's right. And I got that drum in there, but it got lost. Went all around, and I had to write back to em, you know, and they'd write back to me, and they'd trace it. And it'd take exactly six months for that drum to come. I had never had my hand on a drum seat before. Would you believe it or not? That's not true.
You didn't have any hand on a drum seat before. Can you imagine?

It started right out as a good set then. Yeah, it started right out with the Wallachs drums. That's right. You must have been kind of nervous. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. How old people can tell you about it? That's right.
What kind of a snare drum was it? It was the whole set of drums. The whole set.
The whole set. The whole set, huh? Because it was a different time, it cost me around $110 at the time. Yeah. That's right. What did you say? Come right on in.
Let me follow you. Let's do it. Hold on. Let's do it.
Wallachs drums, as you know, they're... I don't know about now, but they're... at those times, they had good products. They were really good. They're really good.
It's a good company. They've gone into jukeboxes now and electric organs mostly.
Yeah, that's what they go for now. But sometimes, yeah.
What did the set consist of? How many drums and cymbals and so on?
Naratantant. Two drums. Tamarine. What, tamarine? Yeah, tamarine. That's right, tamarine.
Tamarine, a bass drum and a snare drum.
Bass drum, snare drum and a drum stand. How many cymbals? Any cymbals? Yeah, and one cymbals. That's right. All the cowbells and the cymbals. No. They had cowbells with it. Yeah.
Them kind of drum just come with some trays on top of it. Huh? Did they have any wood blocks with it?

No. I think I got the wood block here. When I got here. There was the four wood blocks on top. I got the blocks here. I think I did. I'm not sure. Yeah, I had the blocks, but I got the blocks. That didn't come with the set. I got the blocks here. We used to use them every time they would block. They were right sure. That's right. You used them four cowbells. Four cowbells. Now the cowbells came with the drums. That's what came with the drums. The cowbells, yeah. Was it a set of four cowbells?

Four, yeah. It was a set of four. Yes. They had four. The next size, the next size, the next size. That's right. We always had called him Alexis. I couldn't find him. Who is that? Alexis, Rickard's brother. You know. You used to call Rickard, Rickard. The other one, Kingston, by his name. But when he was taught by the drum, he always said Alexis.
Yes, he still don't know his first name. He said Alexis, yeah.
He was on the election, yeah.

It's possible that Rickard may have told us. We interviewed him a few years ago. Yeah, he put it out on him. That's right. Maybe we already have it on tape, so don't worry about it at present. You probably might have it already. Yeah, we may have it. We did interview Rickard. We talked about his family as much as we could remember to ask him about it. I was going to ask some more about Buddy Petit. How did he play? Was he really good? Some people say he was very good. I was just wondering if he was one of the best, or what did you say?
He was one of the best, or what did you say? He had his own style. He had his own style. He didn't. But he had his own style.
Is he extra loud, or fast, or high, or low, or any special things about the way he played?

Well, I'll tell you about Buddy. Buddy, for you some of all kind of choppy. For you the beautifulest. I see you down on, what's this one? Is that an example? That goes to Richland? Yeah. Is that a example? Yeah. If I ever go to Richland. No, that's LaFouche. If I ever go down on LaFouche, yeah, Buddy LaFouche is there. I see you down on Buddy LaFouche, and those people were playing with the white dancers, and his brothers playing, during this time, his voice came out, my buddy. You know, they used to preach to him on that. And that man could play the sweeter music, you know, on that trumpet. It's soft and sweet. It's the best he could play loud, or the hot.
